extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic / philosophy of language; teachers and philosophers concerned with the theory of names and meaning
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic taxonomy and explanatory guidance for different kinds of names (proper, connotative, relative, privative, etc.) and how their signification, connotation, and usage affect meaning and precision in discourse. Aimed at clarifying how to fix connotation for accurate thinking and argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names (unmeaning marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names (e.g., Brown, York) are unmeaning marks which serve merely to show what individual thing is being talked about; they do not, properly speaking, convey any information about the object (they connote nothing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper names function like a distinctive mark (analogy: chalk mark on a house) attached to the idea of an object to allow identification in discourse or record; by themselves they enable identification only, and any further information comes from prior acquaintance with the name, not from the name's meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotative names (general concrete names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Connotative names are names that, besides denoting objects, connote attributes — the meaning of such names resides in what they connote rather than merely in what they denote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'built of marble' conveys new information purely by its signification; connotative names are significant marks (a 'livery' of the attribute). They should be treated as names of all the individuals they are predicable of, and one must attend to their connotation to know their meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotative individual names (individual but connotative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some names are individual (predicable of one object) yet connotative in that their meaning implies an attribute or condition that only one object possesses (e.g., 'the only son of John Stiles', 'the first emperor of Rome').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such individuality may be implied by the definite article 'the' or by context; examples: 'the father of Socrates' (uniquely individual because of the fact), 'the author of the Iliad' (individualized by asserted fact). Note that words like 'the sun' or 'God' may appear individual but are, in strictness, general in meaning unless the connotation itself includes uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many-worded names and context-individualization
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex name can consist of a general name limited by additional words so that the full expression is predicable of only one object (e.g., 'the present prime minister of England').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general term supplies a class and the limiting words (time/context) narrow it to an individual; context or the article 'the' can individualize otherwise general expressions (e.g., 'Caesar's army' in a particular battle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indeterminate (vague) connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some general names have a connotation that is unsettled or vague (we do not exactly know how much a word connotes or what degree of a quality suffices for application) — e.g., 'man' (uncertainty about precise external form or minimal degree of rationality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vagueness can be harmless or useful (e.g., natural history grouping by resemblance) but is dangerous for precise thinking. It leads to lax habits of thought when connotative terms are used without a distinctly ascertained connotation. Philosophers must guard by fixing connotations where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition as the means to fix connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: To remedy indeterminate connotation, one should give a definite and fixed connotation to frequently used general concrete names by defining them, thereby clarifying what attributes are intended when the name is predicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions should aim to fix connotation with minimal change to the habitual application of the word and with the least disturbance to accepted true propositions; the process is delicate and central to clearer philosophical discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: indeterminate connotation vs multiple fixed connotations (ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names with indeterminate connotation (vague meaning) differ from ambiguous words that have more than one fixed, recognised meaning (e.g., 'post', 'box').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous words can be treated as multiple names (distinct senses) and distinguished clearly to avoid confusion; indeterminate connotation requires fixing by analysis or definition rather than merely distinguishing senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive and negative names
rubrics_metrics.description: Names may be classified into positive (e.g., man, tree, good) and negative (e.g., not-man, not-tree, not-good); every positive concrete name can have a corresponding negative name denoting everything except that thing or class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative names connote the absence of an attribute, which itself is an attribute (e.g., 'not-white' denotes all things except white things and connotes the attribute of lacking whiteness). Negative concrete names may have corresponding negative abstract names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privative names
rubrics_metrics.description: Privative names denote something which once had, or might be expected to have, a particular attribute but does not (e.g., 'blind'); they connote both the absence of certain attributes and the presence of others from which the absence would have been expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privatives are equivalent to a positive and a negative taken together in signification: they imply an original reference-class (things that normally possess the attribute) and assert the absence of that attribute in the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form vs reality of positivity/negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: A word's grammatical or morphological form (positive or negative) does not always match the reality of what it signifies: some words positive in form express a negative reality and vice versa (e.g., 'inconvenient' positive in form but not mere absence of convenience; 'idle' positive in form but equivalent to 'not working').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care is needed in analyzing signification: do not assume form determines logical status; examine whether the term connotes presence, absence, or other positive attributes (examples: 'unpleasant' connotes positive attribute of causing annoyance; 'sober' may be read as 'not drunken').

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative and non-relative names (definition of relative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative names (e.g., father, son, like, equal, cause, effect) are always given in pairs and, besides denoting an object, imply the existence of another object; a name is relative when its signification cannot be explained without mentioning another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative names connote a set of facts (a series of events) in which two individuals are implicated — the schoolmen called this the 'foundation of the relation' (fundamentum relationis). One may predicate the related attribute of either party by describing the same fact from different aspects (father/paternity vs son/filiation). Relative names thus depend on that underlying fact/series of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Univocal, equivocal, and analogous/metaphorical use
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is univocal when applied in the same sense to all things it predicates of; equivocal (ambiguous) when applied in different senses (effectively multiple words); analogous/metaphorical when applied in related but not identical senses (derived secondary meaning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivocal words are better treated as distinct names coinciding in sound; analogous/metaphorical uses derive a secondary sense from a primary one (e.g., 'brilliant' light vs 'brilliant' achievement). A common fallacy arises when one reasons from a metaphorical (secondary) sense as if it were the literal (primary) sense.
